thread.title: After the Bell: Trade and Tech Dominate This Market

author: Teresa Rivas
title: After the Bell: Trade and Tech Dominate This Market
text:
By Teresa Rivas July 26, 2018 5:25 p.m. ET The Dow Jones Industrial Average was the only index to notch gains on Thursday after Facebook's (FB) downbeat earnings destroyed all its 2018 gains , and walloped other tech stocks. Now imagine how bad it would be if we didn't have a potential trade-war-ending agreement to celebrate. In today's After the Bell we...
...check where we are in the tariff tussle; ...check in on Facebook's earning woes; ...highlight a strong day for Advanced Micro Devices . Illustration: Getty Images Sending a Friend Request to Europe
The Dow Jones Industrial Average was the only index to end higher on Thursday, basically because Facebook (FB) isn't a component.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 112.97 points, or 0.44%, to 25527.07. The S&P 500 lost down 8.63 points, or 0.30%, to 2837.44. The Nasdaq Composite
You could be forgiven for thinking that Facebook's earnings were the only piece of news today, and there were plenty of headlines, from the fact that investors want to strip founder Mark Zuckerberg of his chairman title to the warning that it may have to take the drastic step of paid subscriptions , and of course worries about whether or not Facebook's fall would hurt other FAANG stocks , a group that also includes Amazon.com (AMZN), Apple (AAPL), Netflix (NFLX), and Alphabet (GOOGL).
Yet that wasn't all that was on investors’ plates. There's still the news that the U.S. may have sidestepped at trade war with Europe and gained an ally in pressuring China.
Still, Commonwealth Financial Network's Brad McMillan notes that there's no deal in place, just a promise to work things out—a positive development, for sure, but not a definitive agreement. Moreover, the China-U.S. trade war is the more pressing issue, and while Europe may prove a valuable player to have on America's side as it spars with China, its help is not assured. "Trade risks remain very real,” says McMillan. “So far, markets have not really reacted. But that could change if the recent good news reverses."
The stakes are high, given that the bull market is long in the tooth but economic data and strong corporate earnings have thus far been able to beat back any downturn. Yet the trade war (or lack thereof) will likely be the determining factor in whether or not the second-quarter earnings season marks a peak in growth, says CFRA's Lindsey Bell .
She writes that economic and corporate fundamentals are still solid, and that the reactions to this earnings season show fundamentals "still matter to investors." At the moment, they're allowing investors to look past trade conflicts, given that the actual tariffs implemented have been relatively small.
"Resolving trade issues near-term will be the best way to prevent the discussion and reality of economic growth peaking,” says Bell. “An escalation of trade actions is the largest risk to growth going forward."
That's not surprising, given how interconnected the global economy has become. Indeed, we're witnessing the end of an era, writes Joe Quinlan of U.S. Trust , one in which geopolitics were based on conventional military power to one of geo-economics, in which countries fight for their foreign security and national interest goals with "markets, currencies and commerce, rather than with missiles, submarines and drones."
That fact is evident by the very "blatant" way Washington has used its economic might and resources to get what it wants. Tariffs, says Quinlan, are "war by other means."
Yikes. Yet while "combat through economic means" can certainly be destructive, there's still upside, argues Quinlan, as the era of geo-economics may reconfigure the global economy, leading to a more open market in China and the updating of multilateral agreements, which would be good for U.S. companies.
"The markets sense that in the new unfolding era of geo-economics, the U.S. will emerge a clear winner," he concludes. "Stay tuned."
Don't touch that dial!
The Hot Stock
Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) shot to the top of the S&P 500 today after the second quarter results topped analysts expectations.
AMD was up $2.30, or 14.33%, to $18.35 .
The growth in the second quarte r was driven by new products such as Epyc, and the company’s Ryzen processors for mobile and desktop PCs. “The company lowered its revenue forecast this quarter after a slowdown in graphics cards from the cooling cryptocurrency demand,” said Benchmark analyst Mike Burton .
The shares have climbed 78.5% year to date and 31.5% for the past year.

The Biggest Loser
Nielsen Holding (NLSN) slumped to the bottom of the index after reporting a disappointing quarter.
The global data collection firm lost $7.46 or 25.2%, to $22.11.
The company lost a quarter of its market value after a series of bad news today. After a drop in revenues, the company lowered its annual financial targets for the second half of the year. Nielsen also announced that its Chief Executive Mitch Barns would retire by year-end.
Nielsen is down 39.2% year to date, and it's slipped 47.1% in the past 12 months.
